title: Zustand basics: create, selectors, set, persist

questions.prompt: What does `const useCounter = create<CounterState>((set) => ({ … }))` give you?

options.text: A hook you call with a selector — and the store itself, via useCounter.getState() / setState() / subscribe()
A provider component you must wrap the app in before any component can read the store
A React Context object, which you read with useContext
A store class you instantiate once per component

questions.explanation: `create` returns a hook that is *also* the store: `useCounter(selector)` inside React, `useCounter.getState()` outside it. No provider is needed — the store is a module-level singleton, which is exactly why it's app-lifetime state (and why tests must reset it).

questions.prompt: `const { count, name } = useStore((s) => ({ count: s.count, name: s.name }))`. Why does this component re-render on unrelated store changes?

options.text: The selector returns a brand-new object each call, so the Object.is comparison always fails
Because the component isn't wrapped in React.memo
Destructuring a hook result always disables the subscription optimization
Selecting two fields is unsupported; a selector may only return one value

questions.explanation: Zustand compares the previous and next *selected value* with `Object.is`. Two structurally identical objects are never `Object.is`-equal, so "has it changed?" is always yes. Fix it with two atomic selectors, or one selector wrapped in `useShallow` when you really need an object.

questions.prompt: State is `{ filters: { status: "open", page: 2 } }` and you call `set({ filters: { status: "closed" } })`. What is `filters` afterwards?

options.text: { status: "closed" } — page is gone, because the merge is only one level deep
{ status: "closed", page: 2 } — set deep-merges nested objects
Zustand throws, because partial updates must include every nested key
Unchanged — you must use the functional form to update anything

questions.explanation: `set` shallow-merges at the top level only, so a nested object is replaced wholesale and `page` is lost. Spread it yourself: `set((s) => ({ filters: { ...s.filters, status: "closed" } }))`.

questions.prompt: When must you use `set((s) => …)` rather than `set({ … })`?

options.text: Whenever the next value depends on the current one — it reads the state at apply time, not at call time
Always; the object form is deprecated
Only inside async functions
Only when the state has nested objects

questions.explanation: Same reasoning as functional updates in `useState`: `set({ count: count + 1 })` uses a value captured earlier, so two rapid increments can collapse into one. `set((s) => ({ count: s.count + 1 }))` reads the freshest state when the update is applied.

questions.prompt: Why does a persisted store usually need `partialize`?

options.text: To persist only the data — otherwise the store's action functions are serialized too, and the junk comes back on rehydration
To make writes to localStorage asynchronous
It's required; persist throws without it
To encrypt the persisted payload

questions.explanation: `persist` serializes the whole state by default. Functions don't survive JSON, so you store noise and can end up merging junk keys over your real actions after rehydration. `partialize: (s) => ({ theme: s.theme })` persists exactly the data you meant to keep — and shrinks what you have to migrate later.

questions.prompt: A persisted theme store in a server-rendered app renders the wrong theme for a frame and logs a hydration warning. Why?

options.text: The server rendered the default (no localStorage there), so the client's first render must match it — apply the persisted value only after mount
A Zustand bug; persist doesn't support SSR
localStorage reads are async, so the value always arrives after paint
Because the store isn't in a Context provider

questions.explanation: Hydration requires the client's first render to produce the server's markup. The server has no localStorage, so it emits the default; rendering the persisted value immediately mismatches. Gate on `hasHydrated()` (or a mounted flag) and render the persisted value on the second pass. This is the same hydration gate any localStorage-backed state needs.

questions.prompt: Two tests interfere: the second one starts with the count the first left behind. What's the fix?

options.text: Snapshot the initial state at import and `useCounter.setState(initial, true)` in beforeEach
Nothing to fix — each test file gets a fresh store automatically
Mock the zustand module in every test
Wrap each test in a store provider

questions.explanation: A module-level store is created once per module registry and shared by every test in the file — that's the flip side of "no provider needed." Reset it explicitly between tests; the `true` second argument replaces the state instead of merging, so nothing from the previous test survives.

prompts.prompt: Create a counter store whose increment reads the previous value.
prompts.explanation: `create` builds the hook/store from an initializer that receives `set`. The functional form of `set` reads the current state when the update is applied, so rapid increments don't collapse.

prompts.prompt: Subscribe to just the count, so unrelated store changes don't re-render this component.
prompts.explanation: An atomic selector returns a primitive, so `Object.is` can tell whether it actually changed. Calling `useCounter()` with no selector subscribes to the whole state and re-renders on every change.

prompts.prompt: Read and write the store from plain, non-React code (a test, an event handler in a module).
prompts.explanation: The hook is also the store object: `getState()` reads the current state (actions included) and `setState()` writes it — no component, no renderer. This is what makes a Zustand store straightforward to unit test.

prompts.prompt: Persist only the theme under a named storage key.
prompts.explanation: `persist` wraps the initializer; `name` is the storage key and `partialize` narrows what gets written so the store's functions aren't serialized. Note the curried `create<Settings>()( … )` — that extra call is what keeps TypeScript inference working through middleware.

snippets.question: Does CountLabel re-render?
snippets.explanation: The selector returns a *new* `{ count }` object on every call, so Zustand's `Object.is` check always reports a change — you get the Context behavior you were trying to avoid. `useStore((s) => s.count)` returns a number and re-renders only when the number changes.

snippets.question: What is logged?
snippets.explanation: `set` merges only the top level: the whole `filters` object is replaced, so `page` disappears. Spread the nested object yourself — `set((s) => ({ filters: { ...s.filters, status } }))`.

snippets.question: What is count afterwards, and what would the functional form give?
snippets.explanation: Both calls captured `count === 0`, so the second write clobbers the first with the same value — the classic lost update. `setState((s) => ({ count: s.count + 1 }))` reads the state at apply time and lands on 2. Same rule as functional updates in `useState`.
